translation: Hence in treating wasting-thirst, one supplements the vacuity of the yin-cold of kidney water, drains the repletion of the yang-heat of heart fire, removes the excess of dryness-heat in the intestines and stomach, and relieves the decline of the fluids of the whole body, causing the pathways to be dispersed and not knotted, the fluids to be generated and not dried up, and the qi and blood to be free-flowing and not astringent; then the disease daily resolves. (Dispersing the knotted, moistening the dried, and freeing the astringent are the subtle essentials of treating wasting-thirst, and are also the standard rule for treating all diseases. The above discussion of the root qi of the Five Phases of the viscera and bowels is the first section.) Moreover, wasting-thirst is originally brought about by improper diet and nourishment, the intestines and stomach becoming dried up, and the qi and fluids not being able to be dispersed and leveled; or by exhausting and disturbing the spirit, exceeding its measure; or by a major illness, in which the yin qi is damaged and the blood and fluids decline and become vacuous, and the yang qi is fierce and dryness-heat becomes depressed and excessive. Hence the Jizhong (濟眾) says: the three wasting-thirsts all arise from long indulgence in salty things, unrestrained eating of roasted and broiled food, and excessive drinking of wine.
translator_notes: 服館 likely a scribal variant of 服餌 (taking food/medicines); rendered as diet and nourishment.
濟眾 (Jizhong) is a book title, kept with characters.
